items.title: 9 dead, 17 believed trapped after flood hits an unauthorized gold mine in Indonesia
items.description: Rescuers in Indonesia recovered more bodies from an unauthorized gold mine Wednesday and searched for 17 other miners believed trapped inside by flooding, raising the confirmed number of deaths to nine.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[In this photo released by Indonesia's National Search and Rescue Agency (BASARNAS), rescuers inspect a hole where miners are believed trapped by flooding in an unauthorized gold mine in Bogor, West Java, Indonesia, Wednesday, Nov, 25, 2026. (BASARNAS via AP)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Basarnas</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Rescuers in Indonesia recovered more bodies from an unauthorized gold mine Wednesday and searched for 17 other miners believed trapped inside by flooding, raising the confirmed number of deaths to nine.
items.body:
JAKARTA, Indonesia — Rescuers in Indonesia recovered more bodies from an unauthorized gold mine Wednesday and searched for 17 other miners believed trapped inside by flooding, raising the confirmed number of deaths to nine.

The miners were digging for grains of gold late Monday when heavy rain caused the nearby Ciseureuh River to overflow into a mine shaft in the Bogor regency of West Java province.

The shaft, estimated to be about 100 metres (330 feet) deep, is located in a mountainous area south of the capital, Jakarta.

Eleven miners escaped from one section of the excavation before floodwaters filled the shaft, West Java police spokesperson Hendra Rochmawan said. Local miners and residents initially tried to pump water from the site themselves before the situation became unmanageable.

Authorities were not immediately notified because the miners were operating illegally, officials said.

“The problem was that nobody reported it and nobody wanted to report it because the activity was illegal,” said Muhammad Adam Hamdani, head of emergency and logistics at the Bogor disaster mitigation agency.

Rochmawan said police first received reports of trapped miners about 16 hours after the flooding occurred. After an initial assessment by local authorities, firefighters and other agencies, state-owned mining company PT Antam forwarded a formal report to the Jakarta Search and Rescue Agency shortly after midnight Wednesday, triggering a full-scale rescue operation.

The search and rescue team used submersible water pumps to suck water from the hole and tried to close off openings where groundwater seeped in.

“Water inside the hole has not yet receded and is expected to take a long time to drain,” Jakarta Search and Rescue Agency chief Desiana Kartika Bahari said.

She said high water levels, narrow access, slippery terrain and limited lighting complicated rescue efforts. The search operation involves 325 rescuers, including emergency workers, police, the military, health officials and volunteers.

The first victim was recovered shortly after midday, followed by two others about an hour later. Rrescue teams retrieved six more bodies as of Wednesday evening from two adjacent mine shafts. All nine were found dead at depths of 30 to 70 metres (100 to 230 feet), Bahari said.

The flooded shaft was near facilities operated by PT Antam’s Pongkor gold mining unit, but the company said the incident occurred at an unauthorized mine and was unrelated to its operations.

Antam said all of its employees were safe and operations continued normally. The company said it has repeatedly shut access to illegal mining sites in the Pongkor area and uses patrols, drones and surveillance cameras to deter unauthorized mining.

“On humanitarian grounds, Antam is supporting search and evacuation efforts,” company spokesperson Wisnu Danandi Haryanto said.

Informal mining operations are common in Indonesia, providing a tenuous livelihood to thousands who labor in conditions with a high risk of serious injury or death.

Landslides, flooding and tunnel collapses are just some of the hazards facing miners. Much of gold ore processing involves highly toxic mercury and cyanide, and workers frequently use little or no protection.

Niniek Karmini, The Associated Press

items.title: Canada’s foreign student restrictions test Carney’s push to attract research talent
items.description: Canadian universities are working to send a message that they still want international students, after the government’s reduction of student study permits curbed international applicants and took a financial toll on colleges.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Prime Minister Mark Carney rises during question period on Parliament Hill in Ottawa, Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Adrian Wyld]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Adrian Wyld</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Canadian universities are working to send a message that they still want international students, after the government’s reduction of student study permits curbed international applicants and took a financial toll on colleges.
items.body:
TORONTO -- Canadian universities are working to send a message that they still want international students, after the government’s reduction of student study permits curbed international applicants and took a financial toll on colleges.

Less revenue from international students has resulted in staff and program cuts at polytechnic and public colleges and may undermine Prime Minister Mark Carney’s $1.7 billion (US$1.19 billion) effort to attract top research talent to Canadian universities.

Canada’s latest immigration plan targets 150,000 new international student arrivals each year for the next three years, down sharply from 292,830 new arrivals in 2024. The government says the reductions are intended to ease pressure on housing and public services.

“These study permit caps really tarnished Canada’s brand,” said Joseph Wong, vice-president international at the University of Toronto, who has travelled to India three times in the last two years on recruiting trips. “It gave the impression that Canada was closing its doors to international students.”

Carney’s government hopes to attract international researchers who have for decades favoured U.S. universities with larger research budgets. Since U.S. President Donald Trump returned to office last year, his administration has cut or threatened to cut funding from some universities.

Competition with other countries

Robert Asselin, chief executive of the U15 Group that represents Canadian research universities, said Ottawa had exempted graduate students from some restrictions on foreign students starting this year, but warned the changing rules might broadly deter talent.

“What is really important is that we recognize this is something we’re in competition with other countries, and that if we don’t attract these high-quality students, they will go elsewhere, and we will lose talent,” Asselin said.

Canada has committed more than $625 million to attract researchers through newly created research funding programs, with more recipients expected to be announced in early 2027, according to the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada.

The research council referred a request for comment to Canada’s industry ministry. The ministry, which oversees the research council, did not respond to a request for comment.

Open to talent

Canada, beginning under former Prime Minister Justin Trudeau, reduced the number of international study permits partly in response to fraud the government discovered in student visa permit applications. Reuters reported last year that Canada rejected most Indian study permit applications in August 2025. India has been Canada’s top source of international students over the past decade.

“The challenge is actually conveying to prospective Indian students that our door is open,” Wong said of his latest India recruiting trip.

The University of British Columbia warned that frequent policy changes have created uncertainty for students considering Canada.

“Federal policy changes since 2023, alongside global economic challenges, rising geopolitical tensions and heightened competition, have affected international student enrollment across Canada,” UBC spokesperson Thandi Fletcher said.

At Humber Polytechnic, one of Canada’s largest publicly funded colleges, international enrollment for the 2025-26 academic year has fallen to about one-third of 2023-24 levels following federal immigration reforms, according to spokesperson Andrew Leopold. The college faces a $40-million revenue shortfall, resulting in canceled programs and voluntary staff exit packages.

Canada’s immigration ministry said new international student arrivals between January and July 2026 were down 80% compared with the same period in 2024. “With fewer opportunities available, we’re being more selective,” IRCC said in a statement.

(Reporting by Wa Lone; Editing by Caroline Stauffer and Rod Nickel)

items.description: U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration is planning to hike tariffs on Chinese goods by an additional 20 per cent and raise import taxes on products from the European Union, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and nine other major trading partners.

items._ogDesc: U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration is planning to hike tariffs on Chinese goods by an additional 20 per cent and raise import taxes on products from the European Union, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and nine other major trading partners.
items.body:
WASHINGTON — U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration is planning to hike tariffs on Chinese goods by an additional 20 per cent and raise import taxes on products from the European Union, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and nine other major trading partners.

The new tariffs are meant to discourage excessive manufacturing output in those economies, boosted by subsidies and other trade barriers that the Republican administration says put American manufacturers at a disadvantage. The taxes are also intended to help replace the tariff revenues lost after the U.S. Supreme Court ruled in February that Trump could not declare an economic emergency to bypass Congress and impose across-the-board tariffs.

In a late-night call with reporters on Tuesday, a senior administration official provided details of the planned tariffs ahead of the release of a series of investigations into the trade practices of 12 countries, the 27-member EU and the self-governing island of Taiwan. The official insisted on anonymity as a condition for discussing the reports before they were posted by the U.S. Trade Representative’s office.

The official stressed that the tariffs were still at the proposal stage and did not provide strict timelines on possible implementation.

The tariffs — rolled out early Wednesday, the day before Thanksgiving — represent another controversial twist in Trump’s economic policy. Voters in this month’s midterm elections punished Republicans by handing majorities in the House and the Senate to Democrats, with about two-thirds of voters saying that Trump’s policies had made the economy worse, according to The AP Voter Poll, a sweeping survey of the American electorate conducted in all 50 states.

Trump has promised that the import taxes will bring back manufacturing jobs and reduce the federal deficit, but last year’s tariffs contributed to higher inflation that angered voters and led to calls by Democratic lawmakers to require congressional approval going forward.

Brazil and China will face some of the biggest hits

The Trump administration argues that these countries have helped spur an influx of goods at lower prices that undercut American companies, creating a trade deficit in goods that has recently exceeded US$1 trillion annually.

The legal basis of the planned tariffs is Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which enables the U.S. government to investigate and retaliate against foreign trade practices that violate existing deals, are not justified by market forces or actively discriminate against American goods. The official told reporters that the new tariffs would be consistent with the trade deals that Trump reached last year with dozens of countries after threatening severe tariff hikes.

Brazil was singled out for extra punishment after talks on trade issues stalled, the official said. The U.S. is proposing higher import taxes for raw and refined sugar and a new 10 per cent tariff on aircraft, a move that would hit Embraer, Brazil’s largest aircraft maker.

For some Chinese goods, the new 20 per cent tariff will be stacked on top of other import taxes for a total rate of 45 per cent.

The U.S. and China reached a trade truce last year that is set to expire on Jan. 10. The new tariffs will not come as a surprise to Beijing and are unlikely to undermine the truce, the administration official said.

Trump met last week in Shenzhen, China, with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and plans to host him next month at the Group of 20 summit in Florida, an event at which the truce and issues over access to rare earth minerals and China’s purchases of American agricultural products could be discussed again.

The tariffs won’t stack on top of other taxes on cars and steel

The official stressed that the tariffs are targeted to specific products. They would not stack on top of separate tariffs on automobiles, steel, aluminum and other products that the administration has separately imposed under Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962.

Neither will they stack on top of levies of 10 per cent to 12.5 per cent announced in July for 60 trading partners that the White House said have inadequately enforced bans on goods produced by forced labour.

Other nations facing the new tariffs are Bangladesh, Cambodia, India, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Thailand and Vietnam. The official said there are two other countries with pending investigations: Mexico and Norway.

The Associated Press confirmed the planned tariff announcement ahead of the call, according to people who insisted on anonymity because they were not authorized to comment publicly. The plans were reported earlier on Tuesday by Bloomberg and The Wall Street Journal.

Chris Rugaber, Aamer Madhani And Josh Boak, The Associated Press

items.body:
HONG KONG — Market relief about the improbable return of Nvidia’s Jensen Huang is fading as a rout in the tech sector appears to be heading into a second day.

Questions about Nvidia’s corporate governance, as well as the influence of a U.S. president who owns millions of dollars’ worth of shares in the company, have added to concerns surrounding the artificial intelligence sector.

Futures for the S&P 500 fell 1.6 per cent Wednesday, while futures for the tech-heavy Nasdaq tumbled 2.5 per cent. Futures for the Dow Jones Industrial Average declined 431 points, or 0.9 per cent.

Shares of Nvidia slumped five per cent and shares of Anthropic, which soared to US$115 after the largest initial public offering in history last week, gave up another four per cent to trade around $81.90. Anthropic shares fell below the initial offering price of $83 for the first time on Tuesday.

  • S&P 500 market updates here

Also potentially weighing on markets are expectations that the Trump administration will announce plans to raise tariffs on China and 15 other trading partners. China recorded a record trade surplus of nearly $1.2 trillion last year.

Also, the U.S. will release the October personal consumption expenditures report, or PCE, on Wednesday. The data carries a lot of weight because it is the preferred measure of inflation used by the U.S. Federal Reserve, which is attempting to bring inflation down to its target rate of two per cent.

Economists believe, however, that inflation picked up again in October.

That could weigh on markets, particularly the Nasdaq, though many already expect the Fed to raise its benchmark interest rate at least once in the coming months.

High interest rates are making it more difficult to borrow money to pay for growth in the AI industry. Sweeping victories for Democrats earlier this month in the U.S. midterm elections have raised the possibility of more regulation for AI, potentially slowing construction of data centers.

U.S. markets have become extremely volatile but have mostly been sinking since the Dow and Nasdaq hit all-time highs last month

In European trading Wednesday, Germany’s DAX edged down less than 0.1 per cent to 25,007.20. In Paris, the CAC 40 rose 0.8 per cent to 8,105.03, while Britain’s FTSE 100 gained 0.3 per cent to 10,494.10.

In Asian trading, Taiwan’s Taiex closed down 4.8 per cent at 38,195.43. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. fell 3.6 per cent, while chip designer MediaTek plunged 10 per cent.

South Korea’s Kospi lost 6.2 per cent to 4,697.51 as Samsung Electronics fell 9.9 per cent and SK Hynix plummeted 11.1 per cent.

Japan’s Nikkei 225 dropped 2.8 per cent to 57,011.62. OpenAI investor SoftBank Group slumped 14.8 per cent, while semiconductor maker Kioxia plunged 14.2 per cent.

Hong Kong’s Hang Seng slipped 1.1 per cent to 21,966.01. The Shanghai Composite index declined two per cent to 3,476.47.

Brent crude oil, the international benchmark, fell 0.8 per cent to $88.03 a barrel early Wednesday. U.S. benchmark crude dropped one per cent to $81.21 a barrel.

The U.S. dollar rose to 159.51 Japanese yen from 159.26 yen. The euro slipped to $1.0933 from $1.0966.

items.title: Global airports court private capital to fund upgrades, raising cost concerns
items.description: Global airports are banking on increased private investment to help cover trillions of dollars in expected long-term spending to refresh and expand aging terminals and build new ones, although industry officials warn such ventures risk higher costs.
items._ogDesc: Global airports are banking on increased private investment to help cover trillions of dollars in expected long-term spending to refresh and expand aging terminals and build new ones, although industry officials warn such ventures risk higher costs.
items.body:
MONTREAL -- Global airports are banking on increased private investment to help cover trillions of dollars in expected long-term spending to refresh and expand aging terminals and build new ones, although industry officials warn such ventures risk higher costs.

While private investment has flowed for decades into aviation infrastructure, such partnerships are gaining renewed attention as tight public budgets leave aging airports and control towers unprepared for an expected doubling of passenger travel by 2050.

More than US$4 trillion is expected to be spent over the next 30 years on such infrastructure, according to data from trade group Airports Council International presented at a UN aviation gathering in Montreal last week.

“We need to have investment in the industry and we can’t rely only on government investment, so we need to have private investment,” ACI Director General Justin Erbacci said in an interview.

But airlines and industry groups have raised concerns about partnerships with the private sector, given cases of earlier ventures raising airline fees that carriers typically pass on through higher ticket prices.

In Canada, where the government is seeking private investment for its Toronto, Montreal, Vancouver and Calgary airports, labour groups have raised alarm over higher costs seen in other countries.

Australian airlines have called for increased oversight to cap fees, decades after the government sold airports in Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane and Perth to pension funds and infrastructure investors.

“Private investors need to make a profit, and that money has to come from somewhere,” said Lily Chang, secretary-treasurer of the Canadian Labour Congress.

Indonesia’s InJourney, a state-owned holding company that manages 35 airports as well as hotels, is considering whether to bring in a private partner for the first time, a top executive said.

But control remains a concern because “with airports, we have to think about safety, security, borders into our countries,” InJourney CEO Maya Watono said in an interview. “We are very careful with airports.”

Transparent process

While airlines do not oppose privatizing airports or control towers, they want a transparent process that does not lead to soaring costs, according to airline trade group IATA.

“We as users need to be consulted throughout the process, which is not always the case in many countries,” said Thomas Reynaert, IATA’s senior vice president of external affairs. “At the end of the day we’re getting the bill.”

As airline traffic rises and government budgets tighten, the global proportion of passengers flying through airports with private-sector participation has grown to about 50 per cent, up from 41 per cent a decade ago, according to ACI.

Most private investment has gone into brownfield projects that expand or rehabilitate existing airports because they offer lower risk and provide investors with predictable cash flows. But other countries with fast-growing aviation markets are looking to private investment to support new construction.

Kazakhstan has about eight foreign companies investing in its aviation sector, said Talgat Lastayev, the country’s vice minister of transport. The country is talking with potential private partners for a consortium to build a new airport in its capital Astana, he said.

Lastayev said the country signs investment agreements that give assurances and tax breaks to investors while the government regulates airport fees.

“We always try to keep the balance” between airlines and airports, he said.

Big risk

In Syria, where passengers flying into Aleppo International Airport see bombed-out buildings and crumbled rooftops from the sky before landing on a bumpy runway, the country is attracting some Saudi Arabia-based investors betting on its recovery.

Ahmad BinDawood, a board member at the private-sector Elaf Investment Fund, said it was investing an estimated $1 billion to build a new airport in the city that could support more than 12 million passengers a year and cargo operations.

The project is a bet for the company given conditions after years of war in the country.

“When we started, when we said that we wanted to go to Syria, everyone was skeptical about it and everyone was saying that guys, you are taking a risk,” he said. ”But our bet is that Syria is going to surprise everyone in a very short time.”

(Reporting by Allison Lampert in Montreal; Additional reporting by Joanna Plucinska in Damascus; Editing by Jamie Freed)

LAVAL — Alimentation Couche-Tard Inc.’s net earnings attributable to shareholders came in at US$691.3 million during the second quarter, down from US$740.6 million during the same period last year.

That amounted to diluted net earnings per share of 75 cents US during the period, compared with 79 cents US during last year’s second quarter.

The Laval, Que.-based company, which keeps its books in U.S. dollars, says its revenue reached US$22.5 billion for the period ended Oct. 11, rising year-over-year from US$17.9 billion.

  • Latest updates on company news here

The company says the revenue gain is mainly due to higher average fuel selling prices, organic growth in convenience activities and acquisitions.

In July, Couche-Tard made a US$8.6-billion offer for a controlling stake in the Polish convenience store operator Zabka Group.

Couche-Tard CEO Alex Miller says its offer has received all regulatory approvals and is expected to close on Dec. 7.

items._ogDesc: China Southern Airlines said its subsidiary Xiamen Airlines agreed on Tuesday to buy 50 Boeing 737 MAX 8 planes at a list price of about US$7.4 billion, the largest Chinese airplane deal for the U.S. planemaker in nearly a decade.
items.body:
HONG KONG/WASHINGTON -- China Southern Airlines said its subsidiary Xiamen Airlines agreed on Tuesday to buy 50 Boeing 737 MAX 8 planes at a list price of about US$7.4 billion, the largest Chinese airplane deal for the U.S. planemaker in nearly a decade.

The order follows a commitment for 200 jets that China made during a summit between U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Beijing in May.

Jefferies said in a research note that it understood the planes, to be delivered from 2031 to 2034, represented the first conversion of China’s 200-jet commitment to a firm order.

The U.S. planemaker had been largely shut out of new orders from the world’s second-largest aviation market since 2017 amid trade tensions between Beijing and Washington, though it has still been delivering planes from older orders.

Boeing and Airbus forecast China will require around 9,000 new jets by 2045 to meet demand, more than any other region.

China has not announced any specific orders as part of the 200-airplane commitment, and a China Southern securities filing did not say whether this order was included. Boeing, whose shares rose one per cent on Tuesday, declined to comment.

Airlines typically receive a large discount on the list price from manufacturers.

Trump expects more orders

Trump said on Monday that he thinks China will buy another 250 Boeing airplanes. He gave no details, and Chinese officials have not confirmed any further purchases.

In May, he predicted China could boost its order to as many as 750 planes.

The 737 MAX jets in the Xiamen agreement are scheduled for delivery in batches between 2031 and 2034, China Southern said in the filing, adding that the deal is subject to approval from the company’s shareholders and relevant Chinese government authorities.

China Southern said the order would help Xiamen Airlines seize opportunities arising from its move to the new Xiamen Xiang’an International Airport, support the construction of an aviation hub in Fujian province and optimize its fleet structure.

Xiamen Airlines, historically an all-Boeing operator, ended a nearly four-decade-long all-Boeing fleet in early 2023 when it took delivery of its first Airbus A321neo under an operating lease.

In April, China Southern and Xiamen Airlines also agreed to buy 137 Airbus A320neo family aircraft.

(Reporting by Julie Zhu in Hong Kong, Yukun Zhang, Xiuhao Chen and Ryan Woo in Beijing and David Shepardson in Washington; Editing by Andrew Heavens, Emelia Sithole-Matarise and Jamie Freed)

items._ogDesc: A new report says too many newcomers to Canada are getting stuck in jobs they are overqualified to do, undermining the federal government’s quest to recruit highly educated, highly specialized workers from abroad.
items.body:
OTTAWA — A new report says too many newcomers to Canada are getting stuck in jobs they are overqualified to do, undermining the federal government’s quest to recruit highly educated, highly specialized workers from abroad.

The Institute for Canadian Citizenship’s annual report — “Selected But Neglected” — argues the government needs to do more work on foreign credential recognition in key fields like health care to ensure immigrants who are courted for their qualifications can actually put them to work.

The institute projects half of the 380,000 permanent residents admitted to Canada next year will have a university education, but only 36 per cent of those people will have jobs that make use of their education and qualifications over the next 20 years.

Almost half of those with university degrees — 47 per cent — will hold jobs below their education levels, and almost one in five will leave Canada over the next 20 years, the institute says.

Census data from 2016 and 2021 shows 88 per cent of Canadian-born working-age people are in jobs that match their education levels, while just 62 per cent of immigrants can say the same.

The institute cites a 2019 RBC report that estimates closing the labour gap between immigrant and Canadian-born workers could have boosted Canada’s gross domestic product by about $50 billion at the time. The bank’s economists found immigrants were earning about 10 per cent less than their Canadian-born peers.

The report argues Canada should do more to recognize foreign credentials and professional licensing in key fields like medicine where there are persistent staff shortages.

The institute also calls on the government to do more to track how many immigrants are underemployed and how many eventually leave Canada for other opportunities.

The government does grant preferred immigration access to those with higher education and more work experience in high-demand fields like the trades, medicine and research.

The report’s methodology uses a combination of Statistics Canada, census and long-term immigration data in making projections.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 25, 2026.

David Baxter, The Canadian Press

items._ogDesc: In less than two months, Democrat Hannah Pingree will be sworn in as Maine's new governor, replacing Janet Mills.
items.body:
In less than two months, Democrat Hannah Pingree will be sworn in as Maine’s new governor, replacing Janet Mills.

Speaking to CTV News on Tuesday, she said she plans to continue repairing the relationship between Maine and Atlantic Canada following national cross-border tensions and tariffs implemented by both countries.

“As governor, I certainly hope to work with Canada as much as possible, especially the Maritime provinces,” she said.

“I will be advocating to our federal delegation, to members of Congress and to the White House that this is not good for our economy, it’s not good for consumers, and it’s not good for our friends in Canada,” she said of tariffs.

  • Download the CTV News App for breaking news alerts and video on all the top stories

She acknowledged that as a state governor, the federal response to Canadian trade tensions is outside of her control. But she hopes a “blue wave” of Democrats elected to positions in Congress and the Senate will bring change to a number of federal policies, including tariffs.

“The question is really, how will the president deal with the new Congress? He can still veto legislation, but he needs to pass a federal budget, he can’t shut down government forever,” she said.

“This could be a standoff, but I’m hopeful that we will see change. I think even Republicans in Congress, they see the impacts of this president’s policies. They are not helpful for everyday Americans.”

New Brunswick Premier Susan Holt shares that sentiment.

“I do have some optimism seeing that blue wave happen and for that to include Maine. I think that sends a signal to the president that tariffs aren’t good politics and that Americans were showing that they didn’t support those,” she said.

“It’s hard on the Canadian economy. We want to see the U.S. return to be a reliable trading partner.”

Holt recently returned from a trade mission to Cambodia and South Korea, one she said is part of the province’s efforts to diversify markets while working to improve the relationship with the United States.

“One of the things I’ve been doing is going out to try to find those new customers, new markets across Canada, in other parts of the world so that we can have the kind of good paying jobs here in New Brunswick that allow people to pay the bills and live well,” she said.

‘Come and visit us’

Current Governor Janet Mills made headlines last year for her efforts to encourage Canadians to visit Maine.

Pingree said she’s going to continue to work with other governors to continue the work Mills started, and “do a better job finding alliances.”

“There’s so much that we have in common on fishing, on forestry issues, energy issues. We love to have Canadians come and visit us,” she said.

She will be sworn in on Jan​. 6, 2027.

items.title: Canada Is Borrowing Like It’s In Crisis, Killing Hopes For Mortgage Relief
items.description:

The single-month gain was the third-largest since COVID, and part of a much bigger wave of crisis-like borrowing not seen […]

The post Canada Is Borrowing Like It’s In Crisis, Killing Hopes For Mortgage Relief  appeared first on Better Dwelling.
items._ogDesc: Ottawa is borrowing at a crisis pace without a crisis—pushing federal bond debt to $1.33 trillion and keeping Canadian fixed mortgage rates stubbornly high.
items.body:
Canada may not be in crisis, but federal borrowing suggests it’s in the middle of a pandemic-like event. Statistics Canada (StatCan) data shows a historic surge in Government of Canada (GoC) direct bonds in October. The single-month gain was the third-largest since COVID, and part of a much bigger wave of crisis-like borrowing not seen outside of the Global Financial Crisis (GFC) and the pandemic. This doesn’t just limit the country’s options to respond to the next crisis—it all but eliminates the possibility of fixed-rate mortgage relief.

Government of Canada Direct Bonds Just Hit $1.33 Trillion

Total balance of outstanding federal bond issuance.

Source: StatCan; Better Dwelling.

Total direct bonds surged 1.7% (+$22.8B) to $1.33 trillion in October, up 9.8% (+$118.9B) from last year. After a tame September (+$280M), net issuance made the third-largest monthly jump in dollar terms outside of the 2020-2021 pandemic. It trails only April 2023 and July 2025.

The climb is part of a broader trend of persistently elevated growth. Ottawa’s borrowing has logged 26 straight months of annual growth above 6% after the October gain. Over the past three years, the total has increased a mind-boggling 29.2% (+$301.7B). That’s right. Nearly 1 in 4 dollars of federal bond debt was added within three years, outside of the pandemic.

Canada’s Crisis-Like Borrowing Without A Crisis

Canadian policymakers are borrowing at a crisis pace without a crisis. Over the past 12 months, nominal dollar growth was 40.2% larger than the peak 12-month surge during the GFC. Outside of the GFC (2009-2012) and COVID (2020-2022), the balance hasn’t run this close to 10% annual growth since 1997. That was the tail end of Canada’s 1990s fiscal crunch, just as the last major real estate downturn was bottoming out.

The scale of borrowing won’t be easy to shake off. Since February 2020, the net bond balance has climbed 114.8%, more than doubling from pre-pandemic levels. Following a brief dip in 2023, growth came back with a vengeance—averaging 9.4% y/y over the past 24 months. That’s well above the 2010-2019 average of 6.6% on a much larger base. This has created a structural problem.

The Parliamentary Budget Officer has warned that interest payments will consume almost 1 in 7 dollars of revenue by 2030-31. More borrowing has driven debt-servicing costs to grow 29.5% faster than revenue, according to the agency. That would require nearly impossible revenue growth to catch up.

Ottawa’s Bond Supply Is Bad News For Mortgage Rate Relief

Heavy bond supply is set to put a drag on mortgage borrowing. Unlike variable mortgages that track the Bank of Canada’s overnight policy rate, fixed-rate loans are based on GoC bond yields (primarily the 5-year). The medium- and long-term impact of the bond balance may be abstract and debatable, but the short-term impact is crystal clear. It will limit any downside for mortgage rates, helping to build a floor.

For context, the GoC 5-year bond yield sat at 3.4% this morning, 74 basis points higher than last year. Those hoping for good news ahead of their mortgage renewal may not be so lucky, with BMO telling investors that rate relief is done for this phase of the cycle.

items.title: Mortgage delinquency rate up 31% in Q3, driven by Ontario and B.C.: Equifax report
items.description: TORONTO — A new report suggests there's growing stress among homeowners, with some struggling to keep up with monthly mortgage payments as interest rates rise again.
items._ogDesc: TORONTO — A new report suggests there's growing stress among homeowners, with some struggling to keep up with monthly mortgage payments as interest rates rise again.
items.body:
TORONTO — A new report suggests there's growing stress among homeowners, with some struggling to keep up with monthly mortgage payments as interest rates rise again.

Equifax Canada's third-quarter consumer credit trends report says the national 90-plus day mortgage delinquency rate — defined as missed payments three months in a row — reached 0.32 per cent, the highest since the credit agency started tracking the metric in 2013.

That's up 31.1 per cent year-over-year, mainly pushed higher by missed mortgage payments in Ontario and British Columbia.

"That's the highest we've seen, particularly for Ontario. And it's still going up," said Rebecca Oakes, Equifax Canada's vice-president of advanced analytics, said in an interview.

"That's the biggest concern for us."

The Equifax data echoes the findings of a recent a TD report, which showed Ontario's mortgage arrears have nearly tripled from pre-pandemic levels to approach their 2008 financial crisis peak.

"This reflects elevated mortgage balances and greater sensitivity to borrowing costs," wrote TD economist Maria Solovieva in the report published last week.

Growing pressure on households comes as the Bank of Canada raised its policy interest rate by a quarter of a percentage point to 2.5 per cent last month for the first time in more than three years, amid concerns that higher energy prices could spill into broader inflation.

The move prompted the big banks to raise their prime rates, which is used to set interest rates on a range of loans including variable-rate mortgages.

Equifax estimates about 1.4 million Canadians have a variable-rate mortgage out of a total 9.1 million homeowners. Another 1.3 million consumers also have a home equity line of credit, or HELOC, balance of more than $50,000.

Every quarter-point rate hike adds roughly $860 million a year in interest on variable-rate mortgages, the company estimates.

Oakes suspects mortgage delinquencies will continue to rise in the coming months, depending on changes to interest rates.

"If interest rates stay relatively flat from this point on, I'd expect to see it ease off in the middle of next year," she said.

But if more hikes come in, "it's just going to put additional pressure."

The central bank is expected to make its last rate decision of the year on Dec. 9.

Financial market odds for a quarter-point rate hike was 63 per cent as of Monday afternoon, according to LSEG Data & Analytics.

Oakes said first-time homebuyers and younger Canadians may bear the brunt of rising rates because they tend to carry a higher-balance mortgage.

Still, she said mortgage delinquencies overall are less than one per cent.

"It's quite small, you know, from that standpoint, but of course it knocks on to other types of credit, like credit cards, auto loans," Oakes said.

"That's where those individuals miss the payments first rather than on the mortgage itself."

Bank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem said Tuesday that he doesn't see rising mortgage delinquencies as a threat to the economy.

"Obviously for some people, this is very tough," he said in Toronto at an unrelated press conference. "But for the economy as a whole, it's not a huge headwind."Credit card balances reached $136.2 billion in the third quarter, up 4.82 per cent from a year earlier, the Equifax data showed.

Overall, total Canadian consumer debt was $2.74 trillion in the third quarter, up 4.68 per cent from a year ago.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 24, 2026.

Ritika Dubey, The Canadian Press

items.description: Variable-rate borrowers and condo owners face the sharpest exposure as delinquencies keep climbing
items.content: <p>Variable-rate borrowers and condo owners face the sharpest exposure as delinquencies keep climbing</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639311422146198704.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Variable-rate borrowers and condo owners face the sharpest exposure as delinquencies keep climbing
items.body:
The Bank of Canada's first rate increase since 2023 arrives at precisely the wrong moment for a broad cohort of Canadian homeowners.

Delinquency rates have been climbing without interruption for four years, borrowers who bought near the 2022 peak are sitting on negative equity, and those with variable-rate mortgages are about to feel the latest quarter-point move almost immediately.

New data from Equifax Canada puts the full picture in one number: the national 90-plus day mortgage delinquency rate has reached its highest level since tracking began 13 years ago.

Missed payments across three or more consecutive months climbed to 0.32%, up 31.1% year over year. It marks the sixteenth consecutive quarterly increase.

Ontario and British Columbia accounted for 91% of annual growth in severely delinquent mortgage accounts, while total Canadian consumer debt reached $2.74 trillion in Q3 2026, up 4.68% from the same period a year earlier.

Variable-rate borrowers bear the first blow

Of Canada's 9.1 million mortgage holders, approximately 1.4 million carry variable-rate mortgages.

A further 1.3 million consumers hold a home equity line of credit (HELOC) balance above $50,000.

Every quarter-point rate increase adds roughly $860 million annually in interest costs on variable-rate mortgages and approximately $419 million on HELOCs, according to Equifax Canada.

"A rate increase does not have the same impact on every homeowner on the same day," said Rebecca Oakes, Vice President of Advanced Analytics at Equifax Canada, in Ontario.

"Variable-rate borrowers can feel the impact of a rate increase within weeks, while others may not experience the effect until they renew or refinance. With the Bank of Canada's next interest rate decision scheduled for December 9, the group to watch are those homeowners with the least room to absorb another increase."

Brokers are fielding that pressure firsthand. Joel Fox, chief operating officer of Ownright in Canada, explained in an interview with Canadian Mortgage Professional how compounding renewal costs are bearing down on already-stretched mortgage holders.

"Plenty of people locked in at very low rates a few years ago, and they're now renewing into a much bigger payment. This hike doesn't help," he said.

His advice to clients approaching renewal: "If you're renewing in the next year, start early. Talk to your lender or broker, compare offers and know what your payment will be before the renewal notice shows up."

New Ratehub .ca data shows home affordability declined across all 13 major Canadian housing markets in October as rising mortgage rates increased income requirements for buyers. https://t.co/2l9ocHRMfL — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) November 19, 2026

Negative equity rising among Ontario condo owners

The dollar value of severely delinquent mortgages is growing faster than the actual count of delinquent accounts — a signal, Oakes noted, that larger-balance borrowers are increasingly under strain. 

Negative equity — where the amount owed on a property exceeds its current market value — has become concentrated in specific segments.

Ontario accounts for an estimated 70% of Canadian mortgages currently in negative equity, representing 5% of all provincial mortgages, compared with 1.85% in British Columbia.

Among condo owners, the exposure rises to 7.2%, against 2.7% for freehold properties. For buyers who entered the market in 2022 near the peak, negative equity risk reaches 8.4%.

"Negative equity is still relatively uncommon in Canada, but what stands out is how concentrated it has become," Oakes said.

"For most of these homeowners it isn't an immediate problem as long as they can keep up with their payments. The challenge comes if they need to sell or refinance."

Victor Tran, mortgage and real estate expert at Rates.ca in Canada, described a gradual but sustained upward path for mortgage delinquencies in Canada during a February interview with CMP. 

"I think [delinquencies] will continue to increase as more homeowners renew their mortgages in the next 12 months, 24 months even. But I think it's going to be a slow grind," he said.

items.title: Canadian mortgage market rewards adaptable brokers in 2026
items.description: Max Singh of TMG The Mortgage Group sees opportunity in a year defined by strategic client decisions
items.content: <p>Max Singh of TMG The Mortgage Group sees opportunity in a year defined by strategic client decisions</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0311_638367747040950607.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Max Singh of TMG The Mortgage Group sees opportunity in a year defined by strategic client decisions
items.body:
The Canadian mortgage market is not short of challenges in 2026, but for Calgary-based broker Max Singh of TMG The Mortgage Group (pictured top), difficulty and opportunity are two sides of the same coin.

Singh describes a Canadian mortgage market shaped by affordability pressures, bond market volatility, and a record renewal wave, with the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC) projecting 1.15 million mortgage renewals in 2026, the largest concentration in recent history.

"I would describe 2026 as a year of adjustment and opportunity," Singh told Canadian Mortgage Professional.

"Compared to last year, I've noticed clients becoming much more strategic about their mortgage decisions, whether that's purchasing, refinancing or renewing."

Navigating a shifting lending landscape

Tightening lender guidelines and heightened scrutiny around income verification and debt servicing have defined the operational challenge of 2026 for Singh.

"With bond market volatility, changing lender guidelines and increased scrutiny around income and debt servicing, mortgage brokers need to be more knowledgeable and adaptable than ever," he said.

"I've always believed our greatest value comes from understanding the client's complete financial picture and having the experience and relationships to find solutions when traditional lending doesn't quite fit."

His assessment aligns with CMP's latest market analysis of the risks facing Canadian mortgage brokers.

Lindsay Zwart, Equifax Canada's director of solutions for mortgage and housing, reinforced the point at MortgageFest Canada in Toronto in September.

"Risking a borrower in 2026 does not look the same as risking a borrower in 2016, in 2019, and in 2020," Zwart told delegates.

"As a broker, your two most valuable currencies are your time and your reputation in the industry with your lenders."

Mortgage Professionals Canada's 2026 consumer survey, cited in CMP's 2026 Brokers on Lenders special report, puts broker market share at 38% in 2025, a six-percentage-point annual gain and the highest level on record.

Looking ahead to 2027

Singh expects confidence to build gradually rather than through dramatic rate reductions.

"I'm cautiously optimistic about 2027," he said.

"I believe we'll see opportunities as economic conditions evolve, buyers regain confidence and homeowners continue reviewing their mortgage options. I don't necessarily anticipate dramatic interest rate reductions, but I do expect clients to become increasingly comfortable making financial decisions rather than waiting indefinitely for the perfect market."

CMP's annual ranking of Canada's 75 best mortgage brokers — professionals who collectively moved more than $10 billion — illustrates the relational model Singh champions.

"Whether it's reaching out six to nine months before renewal, conducting annual mortgage reviews or simply checking in, I believe the brokers who invest in relationships, education and proactive mortgage management will be the ones who really thrive in 2027."

The motivation goes deeper than deal volume.

"At the end of the day, we're not just arranging mortgages; we're helping people build wealth, achieve homeownership and make better financial decisions for their families. That's what keeps me passionate about this business," Singh said.

items.title: Ontario mortgage arrears near crisis peak as rates take toll
items.description: A TD Economics report shows Ontario's arrears rate has nearly tripled since the pandemic
items.content: <p>A TD Economics report shows Ontario's arrears rate has nearly tripled since the pandemic</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639311370259041851.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: A TD Economics report shows Ontario's arrears rate has nearly tripled since the pandemic
items.body:
Canadian consumers are expected to "bend, but not break" – but nowhere is that strain more visible than in Ontario, where mortgage arrears have nearly tripled from pre-pandemic norms.

A November report by TD Economics economist Maria Solovieva, CFA, finds the province's arrears rate hit 0.34% in August, approaching the 0.43% peak of the Global Financial Crisis (GFC) from a pre-pandemic baseline of just 0.12%.

While national real consumer spending grew at a nearly 3% pace through the first half of 2026, Solovieva cautions that "solid spending growth masks pockets of financial strain, particularly in Ontario."

Consumer insolvency rates, though still below GFC-era highs, have trended upward since the rate-hiking cycle began in 2022, and the most recent reading "suggests a renewed upward pressure, warranting close monitoring," the report states.

TransUnion's financial stress indicator, also tracked by the Bank of Canada, reached a new high of 2.23% in Q2 2026, roughly 25 basis points above its pre-pandemic average. 

New Ratehub .ca data shows home affordability declined across all 13 major Canadian housing markets in October as rising mortgage rates increased income requirements for buyers. https://t.co/2l9ocHRMfL — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) November 19, 2026

What rising arrears mean for brokers and their clients

Ontario's vulnerability traces to the pandemic housing boom. As CMP's analysis of Ontario and BC delinquency trends confirmed, buyers near the 2021–22 price peak carry larger balances and thinner equity, while BC 's rate of increase has started to slow.

The TD Economics report notes that "even at today's elevated rate, roughly one in 300 Ontario mortgages is in arrears," and that "the greatest vulnerability likely lies among those who purchased near the 2021–22 housing market peak, when prices were highest and equity cushions may be thinnest."

Leah Zlatkin, licensed mortgage broker and LowestRates.ca expert, told Canadian Mortgage Professional in May that the data demands vigilance: "Mortgage delinquency is often one of the last signs of financial strain, because most homeowners will cut back in other areas before missing a mortgage payment," Zlatkin said.

"That's why even a small increase in arrears is worth paying attention to. It can suggest that some households have already used savings, leaned on credit, or reduced everyday spending to keep up. For borrowers coming up for renewal, the question isn't only whether they can make the next payment, but whether payments can be sustained over time."

Statistics Canada data cited in the TD Economics report show more than 35% of households in Oshawa, Windsor, and Hamilton, Ontario are struggling to meet their financial needs – the highest rates among Canada's largest cities – with all three cities reporting unemployment above the national average.

Labour market is the bigger swing factor

The Bank of Canada raised its policy rate by 25 basis points in October, with another increase expected in January 2027.

Variable-rate mortgages account for a historically high 35% of outstanding mortgages in Canada.

The report estimates roughly $115 in additional annual mortgage servicing costs relative to earlier forecasts; in Ontario, the figure rises to approximately $140 annually – on top of a servicing burden already around $2,250 above the national average.

Those increases are "unlikely to be the straw that breaks the camel's back, but they represent another expense for households whose budgets are already stretched by higher inflation," Solovieva writes.

Victor Tran, mortgage and real estate expert at Rates.ca, told CMP earlier this year that a dramatic escalation remained unlikely: "I think [delinquencies] will continue to increase as more homeowners renew their mortgages in the next 12 months, 24 months even. But I think it's going to be a slow grind," he said.

"It's not going to be a significant, drastic increase suddenly and I don't think we're going to see sudden mass foreclosures or power of sales. At the end of the day, the banks and lenders out there are in business to help homeowners out and lend them money, not to foreclose on homes."

TD Economics forecasts Ontario's arrears to plateau near mid-2027, declining in the second half of the year as employment conditions improve.

The principal risk is clear: "if weak hiring gives way to widespread job losses, pushing the unemployment rate higher, mortgage arrears could rise further and remain elevated for longer."

For now, the report's conclusion stands – "households in Ontario and across Canada are expected to bend, but not break."

items.content: <p>Executive tells CMP why the lending giant is backing the prestigious industry awards</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639217273141247328.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Executive tells CMP why the lending giant is backing the prestigious industry awards
items.body:
MCAN Financial Group is backing the 2026 Canadian Mortgage Awards (CMAs) as sponsor for one of its most important honours, the MCAN Award for Woman of Distinction, with the 20th edition of the ceremony set to take place on Wednesday (November 25) at Rebel Toronto.

The awards are an important opportunity to celebrate the people behind an industry that’s as essential as ever to helping Canadians achieve their homebuying dreams, according to MCAN’s director of corporate brand and marketing Kim Mercer.

“MCAN is proud to support the Canadian Mortgage Awards because at its core this industry is about people,” she told Canadian Mortgage Professional. “The CMAs give us a chance to set competition aside and celebrate what we’re all working toward: helping Canadians make it home.”

With mortgage professionals set to congregate in Toronto from across the whole country for the star-studded ceremony, Mercer said the evening was also about connection.

“It’s an opportunity to recognize the brokers, teams and partners who show up for their clients and communities every day, and the people and partnerships that keep our industry moving forward,” she said.

“It’s also a fun night to reconnect with colleagues, celebrate success, and cheer on the award nominees.”

Mercer said the MCAN team is especially excited about the nomination of Cam Dellipizzi, one of 10 shortlisted for Lender BDM of the Year (Prime).

The value of relationships

The case for celebrating excellence comes back to relationships, Mercer said, at a time when the connection between brokers and lenders has arguably never been more important.

“This is a relationship-driven business, and excellence often comes down to how many people show up for their clients and partners, especially when the market is complex,” she said.

The event takes place at a significant moment for the mortgage and housing markets, with affordability challenges and rising interest rates continuing to present hurdles for Canadian homebuyers and owners.

That’s part of the reason mortgage professionals are such a valuable component of the housing sector, Mercer suggested. “After a year of uncertainty, it’s important to celebrate what makes this industry such a powerful part of Canadians’ homeownership journeys: the people,” she said.

“Recognizing great work gives us a chance to celebrate the people raising the bar and reminds all of us what great service and partnership can look like.”

MCAN’s 2026 and 2027 focuses

With 2027 just around the corner, the industry is reflecting on the year that’s been and looking ahead to what’s in store for the coming 12 months.

Mercer paid tribute to the brokers working with MCAN to help Canadians navigate the current market, and highlighted opportunities in store next year. “We’re incredibly grateful for the support of our broker partners and the trust they place in us to deliver for their clients,” she said.

“This year challenged all of us to be more flexible and thoughtful about how we help Canadians navigate homeownership. For MCAN, that means continuing to listen and invest in our people, products, technology and experience, making it easier for brokers to find responsible solutions for real-life client needs.”

On the product side, Mercer said MCAN had worked to keep its mortgage solutions in step with what’s most important to brokers in a constantly evolving market. “A big focus for us has been making sure our mortgage solutions keep pace with what brokers are actually seeing across Canada,” she said.

And the lender has also invested in how brokers work with it. “We’ve continued investing in the overall partner experience through our regional teams, technology, clearer pricing and programs like SCORE and ICON that create value beyond the transaction,” she said.

Meanwhile, the company has kept its partner events going in 2026, with Summits and Connects continuing in Vancouver, Ottawa, Calgary and Spain. Next year’s destination is Porto. “Great partnerships should deliver great business and a little fun along the way,” Mercer said.

As the industry prepares to celebrate its top performers at the CMAs – and toast the importance of strong connections and partnerships – Mercer said the human side of the business remains paramount.

“One thing that continues to stand out to us is that every mortgage file represents a person, a family and a story,” she said. “We believe the good stuff happens when brokers and lenders understand that full picture and work together to find a responsible path forward. That’s the kind of partnership we want to keep building in 2027.”

items.title: Finmo's Sidekick: the AI assistant that knows your deals
items.description: Lendesk's new release takes AI from single tasks to whole deals, and the broker always makes the call
items.content: <p>Lendesk's new release takes AI from single tasks to whole deals, and the broker always makes the call</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0321_639307939243156766.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Lendesk's new release takes AI from single tasks to whole deals, and the broker always makes the call
items.body:
Most brokers have tried AI tools to draft emails and answer quick questions. What they haven't had is an AI assistant that knows their deals and can work on them.

Lendesk built Sidekick to close that gap. Sidekick launched in open beta at Finmo Momentum 2026 on November 24 and it's a new AI assistant inside Finmo, Lendesk's mortgage origination platform. It runs in a chat panel next to the broker's deals, where it reads the application and documents, makes updates on request, and looks up lender rates and guidelines. The broker never has to leave the deal.

“We wanted to give brokers a tool that actually works the deal, instead of just surfacing information about it. Sidekick knows the deal, knows the lenders, and takes on the admin, so brokers can spend more time with clients,” said Carter Zimmerman, president of Lendesk.

From single tasks to the whole deal

Each of Finmo's earlier AI tools did one job. In 2024, Finmo added AI deal create, which builds a new application from an email chain, call transcript or notes, and AI fill from document, which pulls property details from an MLS listing into the deal. This year Finmo added AI down payment verification and income verification, which cut hours of document review down to minutes.

Sidekick works differently. It doesn't run one fixed process. It can help with any task a broker does in Finmo: building and editing deals, managing documents, running down payment and income verification, calculating GDS/TDS, and researching lenders.

“Our first AI tools each solved one problem well. Sidekick ties them together,” Zimmerman said. “For the first time, a broker can ask for help the way they’d ask a colleague and get it across the whole deal.”

Ask Sidekick to organize and review a deal’s documents, and it renames files consistently, moves them into the right document conditions, and adds any missing conditions. It then runs down payment and income verification.

Ask Sidekick which rental income approach works best for a conventional deal, and it compares lenders’ add-back and offset policies using Lender Spotlight. It estimates the impact on GDS/TDS and compares available rates and requirements, helping identify the best fit and the lowest-rate option that meets the lender’s stated qualifying limits.

“Sidekick takes what you thought was a B deal and turns it into an A deal,” said Joe Tomkins, Director of User Development & Enablement at Lendesk.

Placing the deal

Sidekick connects to Lender Spotlight, so it can match a deal against lender policies and pull current rates. The "Place this deal" flow works the deal the way an experienced broker would. It grades the deal, screens lenders on their guidelines, and compares rates. Then it gives one recommendation, with a short list of alternatives.

“Finding the right lender for a deal takes experience, plus a lot of checking rates and guidelines across dozens of lenders,” Zimmerman said. “Sidekick handles the checking in one request, so brokers get to the right shortlist faster.”

The broker makes the call

By default, Sidekick asks before it changes anything. Each update, whether it's an edit to the application or a credit pull, shows up as an approval card with the exact change. Nothing is saved until the broker approves it. Read-only tasks, like reviewing the deal or running GDS/TDS numbers, happen right away.

Sidekick also works within the broker's own permissions, so it can only see and do what that broker already can in Finmo — and brokers can delete their chat history at any time.

“In mortgages, trust isn't optional,” Zimmerman said. “That's why Sidekick shows every change before it's made. The broker is always in control.”

Sidekick is available now in open beta, free while the beta runs. Brokers already on Finmo can ask their team admin to turn it on through Finmo support. Brokers new to Finmo can sign up and request access when they join.

items._ogDesc: Canadian household debt hit $3.3T in September as mortgage growth fell to a 25-year low, while consumer credit ran hot on rising distress borrowing.
items.body:
Canadian household debt is slowing in growth, but it doesn’t appear to be voluntary deleveraging. Statistics Canada (StatCan) data shows household credit climbed in September, though mortgages are contributing less. The segment grew at one of the slowest paces in a quarter-century, even as consumer credit took off alongside rising distress borrowing.

Canadian Household Debt Hits $3.3 Trillion Even As Growth Slows

Annual growth of Canadian household credit.

Source: StatCan; Better Dwelling.

Canadian household debt climbed 0.3% (+$9.4 billion) to hit $3.3 trillion in September, 3.7% (+$119.3 billion) higher than last year. It’s a sharp deceleration from the 4.6% annual growth reported this time a year ago, suggesting household borrowing is slowing. Even at a slower pace, adding over $119 billion in a single year is hardly deleveraging. Households are just lightly tapping the brakes.

Canadian Mortgage Credit Growth Slows To Lowest Pace In 25 Years

Annual growth of Canadian mortgage credit.

Source: StatCan; Better Dwelling.

Mortgage growth appears to be the big drag here. Outstanding mortgage credit rose 0.2% (+$4.9 billion) to $2.47 trillion in September, 3.5% (+$82.6 billion) from last year. This is the slowest annual growth for mortgage credit since mid-2001. In an economy as housing-dependent as Canada’s, a quarter-century low in mortgage expansion signals that buyers are either tapped out or stuck on the sidelines.

Distress Borrowing Keeps Consumer Credit Running Hot At $847 Billion

Annual growth of Canadian non-mortgage household credit.

Source: StatCan; Better Dwelling.

One area of credit growth that continues to run hot is consumer credit. Households grew non-mortgage debt by 0.5% (+$4.5 billion) to $847.0 billion in September, up 4.5% (+$36.7 billion). While slower than August, the annual growth of this segment has been higher than usual over the past few years, sustaining levels the country hasn’t seen since mid-2010. Healthy credit growth can sometimes be a sign of strong consumers, but this isn’t one of those times.

Credit reporting bureaus are increasingly attributing growth to distress borrowing. Firms like TransUnion have noted that more borrowers are carrying higher balances as they use credit to make ends meet. Mortgage borrowers aren’t much better, with the bureau also explaining that a rising share of mortgage debt is due to accumulating balances, not originations.

Slowing headline growth may look like restraint on the surface, but it’s a more ominous sign. There are few signs of relief ahead, as the market expects higher borrowing costs.

items.title: M3’s Bernard talks CMAs, importance of recognizing top performers
items.description: Broker network backs the Canadian Mortgage Awards as brokers gain ground in a tough market
items.content: <p>Broker network backs the Canadian Mortgage Awards as brokers gain ground in a tough market</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639275163379725593.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Broker network backs the Canadian Mortgage Awards as brokers gain ground in a tough market
items.body:
The Canadian Mortgage Awards (CMAs) finally arrive this week – and as the event’s social media sponsor, M3 Financial Group is backing the brokers, lenders, and service providers shortlisted across multiple categories.

The event, set to take place at Rebel Toronto on November 25, will celebrate its 20th anniversary this year. Luc Bernard, chairman and chief executive officer of M3, told Canadian Mortgage Professional that paying tribute to the industry’s best performers was an essential part of ensuring the sector goes from strength to strength.

“We feel that it is of utmost importance to celebrate the mortgage broker industry and recognize the top performers,” he said. Being in a room with the sector’s highest achievers, he said, “obliges us to continue elevating our work year after year.”

The event draws nominations from brokers, brokerages, lenders, underwriters, business development managers (BDMs), and industry service providers across the country. Nominations closed in August, with the shortlisted Excellence Awardees published last month.

Brokers can be recognized regionally, with separate awards for Eastern Canada (Quebec and Ontario), the Maritimes and Atlantic Canada, and Western Canada, or by specialty – with awards for alternative, private lending, reverse mortgage and commercial brokers.

Brokerages and teams compete by size, alongside awards for national broker networks, national brokerages and new brokerages. On the lending side, BDMs and underwriters are recognized in both prime and specialist (alternative and private) categories. Industry service providers, innovators and employers of choice round out the field.

All you need to know about the award categories

Several awards put the spotlight on people. Twelve brokers are shortlisted for Young Achiever of the Year, 11 for The MCAN Award for Woman of Distinction, and nine for The REMIC Award for Finfluencer of the Year, (see CMP's full list of 2026 Canadian Mortgage Awards excellence awardees here).

The fields vary in size. The regional broker awards each have 10 or 11 shortlisted brokers, while the private lending and commercial categories have seven each, the reverse mortgage category three, and the National Broker Network of the Year category four.

Sponsors have also put their names on individual awards, including The EQ Bank Award for Broker of the Year – Reverse Mortgages and The Grechi Carter Professional Corporation Award for Broker of the Year – Commercial. The Haventree Bank Award for Lifetime Achievement, the programme's highest honour, has no shortlist and will be announced only on the night.

Brokers shine in challenging times

The industry’s top performers have shone in a challenging market this year, one that’s brought the importance of mortgage brokers into even sharper focus.

The ongoing trade war with the US, and price pressures caused by the US-Iran conflict, have weighed against the housing market outlook for 2026 as affordability challenges and rising interest rates also leave their mark.

But brokers are coming to the fore in turbulent times that have also seen a wave of mortgage renewals in 2025 and 2026 at much higher rates than the original contract.

Overall broker market share reached 38% last year, according to Mortgage Professionals Canada’s (MPC’s) most recent consumer survey – a jump of six percentage points from the year before.

Nearly two in five Canadians took out their most recent mortgage through a broker in 2025, a new high for the channel, with the share climbing to 48% among recent first-time buyers.

For M3, a key focus of the year has been broker education, with the aim of equipping brokers to be “the best that they can be for future Canadian homeowners.”

Bernard said the night is also a reminder of the bigger goal. “Let’s all work together to grow this industry, allowing more Canadians to trust brokers with the biggest purchase of their lives,” he said.

items.body:
For RFA Financial, returning as a sponsor of the 2026 Canadian Mortgage Awards is not simply a matter of brand visibility — it is an expression of values the Toronto-based lender says are foundational to how it operates.

The awards, presented by Canadian Mortgage Professional, return to Rebel Toronto on November 25 for their 20th anniversary, recognising outstanding work across 26 categories spanning broker, brokerage, lender, and industry segments.

The 2026 edition arrives at what CMP has described as one of the most structurally significant moments in the country's recent mortgage history, shaped by a record renewal wave and persistent affordability pressure from coast to coast.

Among the sponsors backing this year's programme is RFA Financial Inc., the parent company of RFA Mortgage Corporation and RFA Bank of Canada — the firm's prime and alternative lending subsidiaries, respectively.

RFA Mortgage Corporation is sponsoring the Excellence in Philanthropy & Community Service award, a category that Cheryl Buhs, VP of National Sales (Prime) at RFA Financial, says carries particular meaning.

"Our sponsored award, the RFA Award for Excellence in Philanthropy & Community Service, is especially meaningful to us," Buhs told Canadian Mortgage Professional. 

"Giving back to the communities we serve is an integral part of RFA's culture, and it's something we work to champion across the industry."

The recognition of community service within a business-focused awards programme reflects a broader shift visible at the CMAs in recent years.

Buhs said RFA sees its sponsorship as part of a continuing effort to hold up those contributions for wider visibility.

"Supporting this award is one small way we can shine a light on the people making a difference across our country and encourage others to do the same," she said.

Raising the bar across the industry

Frank Giacomini, VP of National Sales (Alternative) at RFA Financial, echoed the view that industry recognition has a practical effect on standards.

"Recognizing the hard work of our peers keeps our industry moving forward," said Giacomini.

"When we celebrate great work, we inspire everyone to raise the bar and find new ways to serve our communities and make homeownership more accessible for Canadians."

Looking ahead to 2027

"Thank you to everyone who continues to put their trust in us. We're excited for what 2027 holds and look forward to building on this year's momentum together."

"RFA is always working to be the preferred lending partner for brokers, and this year has been no different," he said.

"As we close out 2026 and head into 2027, our focus remains the same — finding ways to better serve our broker partners and their clients."

items.content: <p>Tru Cooperative Bank's SVP on sponsoring the CMAs, broker relationships, and a national expansion that crossed the Rockies</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639310566057090312.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Tru Cooperative Bank's SVP on sponsoring the CMAs, broker relationships, and a national expansion that crossed the Rockies
items.body:
When Tru Cooperative Bank agreed to sponsor this year's Canadian Mortgage Awards (CMA), the decision was grounded in something more straightforward than marketing arithmetic.

The federally regulated credit union, formerly known as First West Credit Union, has worked alongside mortgage brokers in British Columbia for more than 23 years — and sponsoring the industry's benchmark recognition event is, in the words of its senior vice-president of pricing and national expansion, Sundar Ramanathan, CFA, (pictured top) a chance to say thank you.

"We have worked with mortgage brokers in B.C. for more than 23 years, and mortgage brokers have played a huge role in our growth," he told Canadian Mortgage Professional.

"Now, as we take our broker business across Canada as a federal credit union, sponsoring the Canadian Mortgage Awards is a chance to say thank you and celebrate the people who've helped us prove that there's an important place for cooperative banking in this industry."

The 2026 CMAs mark the programme's 20th anniversary, a milestone that coincides with one of the most structurally consequential periods in the Canadian mortgage market's recent history. 

The gala takes place November 25 at Rebel Toronto, spanning 23 competitive categories that recognise outstanding work from broker specialists in private lending and reverse mortgages to the teams and technology shaping the market's future.

Results are announced at the awards show and simultaneously published on the CMA website, with coverage in CMP magazine and across its digital channels. mpamag

Raising the bar

Ramanathan makes no distinction between celebrating excellence and improving the broader market.

As a lender that operates on cooperative principles — member-owned, profit-averse in the conventional sense — Tru Cooperative Bank regards recognition events as instruments of collective advancement.

"Mortgages are ultimately a people business," Ramanathan said.

"Great brokers bring advice, trust, and expertise to one of the biggest financial decisions Canadians make. As a cooperative, we believe we're stronger when we help each other succeed. Recognising excellence celebrates the people setting a high standard and raises the bar for the whole industry."

The 2026 Canadian Mortgage Awards is proud to partner with Tru Cooperative Bank in recognizing the Excellence Awardees of the Tru Cooperative Bank for National Brokerage of the Year. #MortgageAwardsCA Book a table: https://t.co/TCt6mK5FV9 https://t.co/M2N4rjG8LI — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) November 19, 2026

A landmark year for Tru

For Tru Cooperative Bank itself, 2026 has been a year of institutional transformation.

First West Credit Union announced on April 1 that it was officially a federally regulated credit union operating under the new legal name Tru Cooperative Bank, with regulatory oversight transferring from the BC Financial Services Authority to the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions (OSFI), placing it under Canada's federal banking regulatory framework.

With this transition, Tru Cooperative Bank became the fourth federally regulated credit union in Canada since federal legislation introduced in 2012 enabled credit unions to operate nationally. 

The broker expansion followed quickly. In May, the organisation announced the expansion of its Mortgage Broker Centre into Ontario through a strategic partnership with MCAP, a Canadian mortgage lender and servicer.

Less than four months after becoming a federally regulated credit union and just 77 days after expanding into Ontario, Tru Cooperative Bank had already exceeded $100 million in approved mortgage volume. 

Provincial growth continued through the year. The move to extend the institution's broker reach deepened a national expansion that gained substantial momentum in Ontario, with Alberta, Saskatchewan, and Manitoba following, and Atlantic Canada identified as the next target market, according to Ramanathan. 

"Our message to brokers is simple: we're here for the long term," Ramanathan said.

"We have 80 years of history behind us, and while our national broker business is new, we aren't. We want to earn brokers' business for the long term by listening, staying competitive and consistent, and being a lender they genuinely like working with."
